title: 'Economic Informed Stock Assessments: Using Prices to Understand the Age of Fish'
authors:
  - name: Min-Yang Lee
    email: Min-Yang.Lee@noaa.gov
    address: [NOAA Northeast Fisheries Science Center, 166 Water Street, Woods Hole, MA 02543, USA]
    corresponding_author: yes
  - name: Emily M. Liljestrand
    email: emily.liljestrand@noaa.gov
    address: [NOAA Northeast Fisheries Science Center, 166 Water Street, Woods Hole, MA 02543, USA]
date: "`r format(Sys.time(), '%B %d, %Y')`" 
abstract: |
 The age-structure of commercial landings is a crucial input to fish stock assessment. In the Northeast United States, NOAA Fisheries deploys samplers to fish dealers to collect length and age information required to construct the inputs.  When there are few or no samples of a market category of fish, stock assessment modelers must make assumptions about these landings, borrow information from different regions or years, or switch to a less-sophisticated model.  The information contained in fish prices can be used to fill data gaps. We use the Black Sea Bass fishery in the Northeast United States to illustrate our approach to using economic data to inform stock assessments.  There are 5 common market categories: Jumbo, Large, Medium, Small, and Unclassified.  From 2020 to 2024, 5 to 10% of commercial landings per year were in the Unclassified market category but no fish in this category were measured or aged. A preliminary hedonic model confirms that prices vary by market category: Unclassified Black Sea Bass are priced between Large and Medium fish. We fit a categorical Random Forest to predict the probability that a transaction belongs to a particular market category using prices and other explanatory factors.  We use the fitted model to predict the probability of the Unclassified belonging to the other four market categories to construct a price-informed age structure of commercial landings. We find moderate differences between the age-structure of the price-informed unclassified landings relative to the status quo method used to in the most recent stock assessment to assign ages to these unmeasured landings.  These findings may have implications for future design of portside sampling programs to maximize the information content and minimize uncertainty of data for stock assessment models.

  - Random Forest

# Introduction

From 2014-2024, no fish in the Unclassified market category of Black Sea Bass (*Centropristis striata*) landed from the south subunit were measured by portside biosamplers in the Northeast United States.  From 2020-2024, no Unclassified fish in the north subunit were measured either.  This left a gap in the data necessary to construct the age-structure of commercial landings, itself a crucial input to the quantitative stock assessments in the Northeast United States. The stock assessment enterprise in the Northeast U.S. has a series of business  rules for handling gaps that arise when certain market categories are not sampled or under-sampled. In this article, we describe a novel approach that harnesses the information contained in the price of fish to fill this data gap.  The economic intuition is straightforward: when consumer demand for fish depends on individual body size, the equilibrium market price provides an informational signal about individual fish size.

In the Northeast US, commercial fishing vessels catch fish at sea, land their catch in a port, and sell their landings to dealers.  Landed fish are sorted into market categories, by vessel operators or dealers.  NOAA Fisheries deploys biological samplers to measure the length of commercially landed fish, and this measurement is typically stratified by market category to guarantee that no group is systematically under- or over- sampled. Otoliths are collected and aged from a subset of measured fish. For Black Sea Bass and many other stocks, these data are used to convert the landed weight of all market categories into numbers-at-age of commercial landings. 

Socioeconomic information has been used in fish stock assessments in limited ways, particularly in the United States. @chan2022 notes five entry points for socioeconomic information in the stock assessment process: data collection, data processing, parameterizing stock assessment models, stock projections, and understanding effects of policies.  Using socioeconomic information in the first three ways remains rare but examples include the use of interviews and participatory modeling with fishing industry participants to inform biological modeling.    [@duplisea2018a ; @duplisea2018b] used semi-structured interviews to reveal that the true catch of redfish (*Sebastes mentella*) was at least twice as high as the officially reported catch; this information was used to select from competing stock assessment models.  Similarly, @Gervasi2025 illustrate how comparable methods can be employed for Gulf Red Snapper (*Lutjanus campechanus*) in the Southeast United States.  A more common pathway for integrating socioeconomic information into the stock assessment process is through standardization of Catch-per-Unit Effort metrics to account for changes due to technology [@walters1996 ; @maunder2004 ; @kleiven2022]. Using prices to fill data gaps is a way to use routinely collected economic data to improve fish stock assessments.

The general goal of this research is to combine economic theory theory and market information to make inferences about difficult-to-observe outcomes; this type of analysis is common in the field of economics.  For example, low variances in bid prices have been used to detect possible collusion [@Abrantes-Metz2006], excess returns on stock option grants suggests backdating of executive compensation [@Heron2007], and underpricing of oil, a violation of the Law of One Price, by Iraq's Oil for Food program suggests sellers were screening for buyers that were willing to pay a bribe [@Hsieh2006].  In this setting, we use information contained in transaction level prices to infer the size of the Unclassified fish. Our research is inspired by, and most closely related to, @Depiper2024's use of a finite mixture model to examine mis-labeling in the Northeast United States quota-managed groundfish fishery. @Depiper2024 note that firms have an incentive to mis-report stocks with high quota costs as stocks with low quota costs. Because firms that mislabel will report a weighted average price based on true and misreported stock; the effects of changes in quantities of the two species on reported prices will be different for non-compliant firms and can be detected statistically.  The incentives to mislabel that motivate @Depiper2024 are not present in this setting; most of this fishery is managed with possession limits and seasonal closures.  Even for the catch share fisheries in three states, there would be no incentive to report a Large Black Sea Bass as a Small.

As part of our exploratory data analysis, we estimate a hedonic model to verify that Black Sea Bass prices in the Northeast region vary by market category. We tune, train, and validate a random forest model that classifies landings into one of the four primary market categories. The goal of this study is to improve the Black Sea Bass stock assessment by including more information about the size of un-measured Unclassified fish. This requires predictions of the Unclassified fish to be aggregated to a level amendable for stock assessment. For Black Sea Bass, this is the year-, subunit-, and semester level and the accuracy of an individual prediction is of no interest.  We use the trained model to predict out-of-sample on Unclassified fish and convert this to an age structure of landings.  Finally, we compare the price-informed age structures to age structure constructed using methods from the most recent stock assessment.

# Background

## Catching, Classifying, and Selling Fish

Black Sea Bass are commercially caught by fishing firms that typically use bottom trawl and pot/trap gear; gillnets and hook-and-line are less commonly used. Firms can target both the size of Black Sea Bass and their catch of other species, but cannot perfectly control what they catch and land.  The ability to target, and therefore the size composition of landings, is impacted by fishing regulations, which vary by state, and environmental conditions. For example, the seasonal inshore movement during the spring and offshore movement  during the fall [@Moser2008-2009] can affect the composition of landings. It can also affect which firms land fish and where they are landed; long trips offshore are unprofitable when possession limits are low. Strong year classes can make a size class temporarily more available during certain years.

The Black Sea Bass fishery is jointly managed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) and the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council (MAFMC). Federal regulations are enacted by NOAA Fisheries. From 1996 through 2003, the fishery was managed primarily by quarterly catch limits for the entire fishery. There were early closures in 1999 (Quarters 2,3,4), 2000 (same), and 2001 (all quarters). Quota was allocated to each state starting in 2003 and is monitored based on landing location.  States enact commercial regulations that ensure landings do not exceed their state's quota. In 2021, the formula that allocates commercial quotas to the states was revised; 75% of the quota is currently allocated according to historical  fishing and 25% is allocated in proportion to the location of the biomass.

Firms operating in federal waters must hold a federal permit; fishing vessel operators are required to report information about fishing trips, including gear used, fishing location, landing locations, and estimates of the weight caught of each species. They are also required to sell their catch to federally permitted dealers, who report information that can be used to link to the vessel reports along with value (nominal dollars) and landed weights (to the nearest pound)^[This has implications for units in subsequent analysis]. These purchase reports are disaggregated by market category.  There is some catch in the nearshore state-managed waters by fishing vessels that do not have federal permits. 

Although all states have enacted some form of Limited Access, there is substantial variability in management across the states. Three states (Maryland, Delaware, and Virginia) currently manage the fishery with an Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) program, while the other states manage with varying combinations of minimum size limits, possession limits, and season closures.  Possession limits vary widely by state; the IFQ states do not have  possession limits while Massachusetts and Rhode Island use seasonally varying limits that have been as restrictive as 50 lbs/day or as liberal as 1,500 lbs per week.

Fishing vessels catch fish and deliver fish to buyers (fish dealers) on land.  The fish are sorted into categories at the time of sale and dealers report transaction-level information about the quantity and value of purchases, disaggregated by market category, to NOAA Fisheries.  For most *ex-vessel* fish markets, including this one, quantity supplied is determined prior to market equilibration; fish are caught and landed before they are sold.  The fish market equilibrates by adjusting prices to equalize quantity supplied and quantity demanded [@Barten1989 ; @Kristofersson2007 ; @Gobillon2017].

The definition of  market categories is not standardized and can vary over time and geography.  Many fish dealers act as wholesalers, selling whole fish to processors, restaurants, or final consumers. Other fish dealers are vertically integrated with some downstream entities, processing and selling filleted fish to downstream customers. Vertical integration, in which a firm has control of the harvest and dealer functions can also occur.  For these observations, the reported prices for these firms are not the result of a competitive market equilibrium.  The market categories exist because downstream buyers care about the sizes of fish; prices of most types of fish depend on the individual body size.   Prices are also influenced by other attributes, including freshness, fat content, water content, buyer- and seller- effects, and the quantity supplied to the market^[@McConnell2000, @Carroll2001, @Kristofersson2004, @Kristofersson2007,  @Lee2014, @Hammarlund2015,  @Gobillon2017, and @Ardini2018 are just a few examples.]. 

There are four prevalent market categories of Black Sea Bass(Jumbo, Large, Medium, and Small), plus an Unclassified category[^aggregation_footnote].  Both panels of Figure \@ref(fig:LengthHistograms) illustrate that fish in the Unclassified category are a combination of the other market categories; based on inspection, they appear to be similar to the Medium category in length, with prices that are slightly higher than Mediums. For both length and price, the histograms have longer tails than the other four market categories.

[^aggregation_footnote]: \label{aggregation_footnote_label} Following the stock assessment, 359 observations Mixed or Unsized were aggregated with the 72,045 observations of Unclassified;  Extra Small (2,962) and PeeWee (8) were aggregated with Small (108,505) category; Extra Large (114) were aggregated with Jumbo (319,859).

Prices can be used to predict market category only if prices actually vary by market category.  A simple hedonic model verifies that prices do indeed vary by market category (Table \ref{HedonicMarketCats}).  The hedonic model is fit by ordinary least squares^[A hedonic price model is not the main focus of this research, nevertheless, we report more details about the simple model in Appendix \@ref(AppendixHedonic).].  In addition to the presented coefficients, the model contains controls for gear, landed state, year, month, daily landings, and the square of daily landings.  All but the final two terms are factor variables that are "one-hot" encoded.  The  Unclassified coefficient (\$9.37) lies between the Large (\$10.28) and Medium (\$8.03), confirming the graphical findings in Figure \@ref(fig:LengthHistograms).  Prices also are monotonically increasing in size.  

## Black Sea Bass and the Stock Assessment Enterprise 

### Stock assessment 

Black Sea Bass are protogynous hermaphrodites, reach maturity around 2-3 years old, and live approximately 8-12 years. They exhibit seasonal movement patterns, overwintering offshore in the fall and winter in deeper waters but returning to inshore waters in early spring to spawn. They prefer to aggregate in structured habitats and are caught near reefs and wrecks. Though Black Sea Bass north of Cape Hatteras are managed as a single stock, a distinction is drawn around Hudson Canyon that subdivides this stock into a northern and southern subunit with assumed, though minimal, movement between these groups which has been confirmed through tagging studies [@Moser2008-2009].

Since 2023, the Black Sea Bass stock assessment model has used an age-based Woods Hole Assessment Model (WHAM) with northern and southern subunits [@Miller2025 ; @nefsc2025bsb].^[Prior to 2023, reference points used by the MAFMC and ASFMC were derived from two Age Structured Assessment Program (ASAP) models, one for the subunit north of Hudson Canyon and one for the subunit south of it.]  Movement between the northern and southern subunit is estimated, with a strong prior derived from *a priori* tagging data [@Miller2025]. Each subunit has distinct assumed life history input like weight at age, length-weight relationships, and maturity at age. The assessment model also estimates distinct parameters for each subunit including abundance, recruitment, fishing mortality, and selectivity. Because the recruitment is distinct, the subunits can have noticeably different size compositions, and the northern subunit had large recruitment events in 2011, 2015, and 2021. 

The assessment model is fit to catch data from the commercial and recreational fishery, and two sources of fisheries-independent indices: model-based indices from a VAST model [@Thorson2019 ; @Hansell2026] and recreational catch-per-angler indices. The conversion from raw catch data to catch-at-age necessitates using portside and observer sampling data of lengths and ages (via otoliths). Because such data can be highly spatiotemporally variable, these data are aggregated to the year, semester (Jan-Jun or Jul-Aug), and subunit (north or south). 

### Port Sampling for Ages and Lengths 

A port sampling program has existed in the northeast United States for more than three decades, collecting vital biological data like lengths, weights, ages, and stomach samples that directly support the fisheries stock assessment process. Sampling is done by professionally trained samplers using electronic measuring boards, scales, and otolith extraction to measure and store the information, often bringing a subset of the samples back to central locations for further analysis like aging.

Throughout its history, the program has been staffed by federal port agents or contracted companies and funded by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS). Because staffing and financial resources are limited, sampling priorities have been set through a two-stage prioritization system.  In the first stage, stocks with analytical assessments, high average recent landings, and high profiles are allocated more samples.  In the second stage, the stock assessment leads use their knowledge of the fishery and assessment to request samples from particular geographices (Maine/New Hampshire, Northern Massachusetts, Southern Massachusetts/Cape Cod, Rhode Island/Connecticut, New York/Long Island, New Jersey or Virginia/Maryland/North Carolina), times of year, and market categories.  These decisions are heavily influenced by availability of historical data, timing and location of commercial landings, spatio-temporal abundance of the stock, and the stock assessment model. The intent when designing the sampling protocol is to provide data necessary to convert landings into an age or length structure through a representative random sampling of landings;  implementation details will necessarily vary on life history and fishery characteristics. 

For the Black Sea Bass stock assessment, the length data sampled at the market category and subunit level is assumed to be representative of all catch from that market category and subunit.  Similarly, the subsampled age data are assumed to be representative of SOMETHING.  Together, these data are used to convert landed weights at the market category and subunit level to numbers at age at the subunit level.[EML Edits needed]

From 2015-2019, the portside biosampling program employed 7 full-time port samplers and collected over 200,000 samples annually. Due to budget reductions and staff attrition, by 2024 fewer than 50,000 lengths were collected by 3 full-time and 3 part-time samplers. The biosampling efforts have been supplemented by partners and stakeholders, like MAFMC and the state of Massachusetts.  A recent merger of the portside sampling program with the NEFSC observer program is anticipated to increase efficiency and sampling, lowering the travel, training, and sampling costs. This merger is also expected to improve logistics coordination and reduce the number of trips samplers need to take from their homes to ports, though this process is still laborious and costly.

Biosamplers try to meet the sample requests by traveling to ports at times when a variety of species and sizes of fish are likely to be landed. They may also travel to a specific port to fulfill the scientific requests for a particular species, stock, or market category. When these requests are unfulfilled, the resultant data gaps necessitate changes in the estimation of commercial landings at age. Modelers will relax the specificity of the information, i.e., borrow across subunits or semesters, and in some cases may take length and age distribution data from fisheries-independent sources rather than from the catch subsamples. However,  unbiased and precise sample information (i.e., that taken from the commercial landings across a broad spatiotemporal range) improves the process of converting the total landings in pounds to landings-at-length and then landings-at-age, which are necessary for age-based stock assessments like WHAM.

Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) illustrates these data gaps and their attendant problems: there are no biosamples for Unclassified fish in the South subunit after 2013 and very few in the north, particularly after 2018^[All measured Unclassified fish in the 2019-2024 time period came from a 2 week span in a single port in 2020.  There are also relatively few samples of Jumbo in the South from 2014-2018 and Small in the North from 2019-2024.].  Conditional on market category, landed fish tend to be slightly smaller in the South subunit relative to the North subunit, reflecting differing regional tendencies for grading.  Filling data gaps in the South with data from the North is therefore likely to produce catch-at-length estimates that are too large. Within a subunit, filling data gaps with an adjacent market category or from an adjacent time period may produce poor estimates of catch-at-length.  

In the most recent stock assessment, contemporanous biosamples from the North subunit were used to fill data gaps for the unsampled unclassified Black Sea Bass in the South subunit from 2013-2020.  From 2021-2024, the length distribution of Unclassified Black Sea Bass in both subunits used data from the North in 2020.  Implicit in this method of filling data gaps is the assumption that data from the donor group (North subunit from 2013 to 2020 or North 2020) are representative of the donee group.  From 2013-2020, borrowing data from the North, rather than a different year, was preferred because it captures changes in annual growth rates.  Other methods of filling this data gap are employed in other stock assessments.  For example, in many of the New England groundfish stocks, when the unclassified market category is missing, the final landings-at-length (calculated from the other market categories) are increased based on the ratio of unclassified landings to total landings.  Implicit in this alternative method is the assumption that combined data from the "Classified" groups are representative of the unclassified group.

# Methods

In this research, we use the transaction level prices to make inferences about the unobserved market category of Unclassified transactions.  Two economic fundamentals guide the modeling approach. First, a perfectly competitive market for fish implies the Law of One Price: homogenous goods will have identical market equilibrium prices.  Second, that *heterogeneous* composite goods can be unbundled into their constituent attributes using a hedonic model and when competitive markets for attributes exist, these attributes will have identical market prices.

## The Competitive Market Equilibrium and the Law of One Price

The existence of a competitive market for Black Sea Bass is critical to our ability to use prices to infer market category.  It ensures that the prices capture all relevant quality information and that there is a single price^[All identical goods will sell at the same price; therefore observations of identical goods with different prices *suggest* that some conditions of a competitive market are absent [@Lamont2003].  Variations of the law of one price that account for heterogenous goods, informational assymmetries [@Salop1982], and different data availability have been proposed and tested statistically [@Asche1999; @Nielsen2009; @Pettersen2018].].  We provide intuition behind the law of one price through contradiction.  A dealer that offers less than the market equilibrium price will purchase no fish because fishing firms would sell to another dealer.  A dealer that offers greater than the market equilibrium price will purchase all the fish and this "too high" price becomes the new equilibrium price.

Many conditions are required for a perfectly competitive market to produce a single price. It requires many small buyers and small sellers, no vertical integration, no transactions costs, and complete information.  Markets with many small buyers and small sellers ensure that no individual can influence the equilibrium price.  No vertical integration ensures that all trades are true arms-length transactions.  A lack of transactions costs means that completing a sale and looking for a counterparty is costless, this enables buyers and sellers to search for the best price.  Complete information ensures that all buyers and sellers know the quality attributes of every lot of fish and the preferences of all the other agents.  Under these conditions, the market prices encapsulate all relevant information.  <!--- We also assume there is no vertical integration between dealers and vessels: a dealer and a fishing vessel is not owned by the same firm and there is no "forward" contracting in which buyers and sellers agree in advance on a price. 
A simple theoretical model sketch can provide guidance about explanatory factors that belong in the model. --->

To build intuition for our model, we temporarily make five further assumptions. First, we assume that all fish in a market category are identical.  Second, we assume that dealers face a downstream customer with a perfectly elastic demand for each market category. These two assumptions imply constant prices for each market category, regardless of the quantity delivered to the market. Third, we assume there are three categories of fish: Jumbo, Large, and Unclassified.  Fourth, the downstream consumers strictly prefer Jumbo to Large, so the market equilibrium price of Jumbo is strictly greater than the equilibrium price of Large: $p^J > p^L$. Fifth, the Unclassified category assumed to be an unknown composite with $\alpha_i$ as the proportion of transaction $i$ composed of Jumbo and (1-$\alpha_i$) Large. 

Buyers and sellers have full information and can observe the proportions of Jumbo and Large in any Unclassified transaction; therefore, the equilibrium price of Unclassified transaction $i$ is:

\begin{equation}
\label{unknown1}
p_i^U= \alpha_i p^J+ (1-\alpha_i) p^L.
\end{equation}

We observe $p^J$, $p^L$, and $p_i^U$; therefore, we can perfectly deduce the composition of an Unclassified transactions ($\alpha_i$).
<!---We assume that dealers have a perfectly elastic demand curve for the two categories of fish, Jumbo and Large, and that they prefer Jumbo relative to large.  A perfectly elastic demand curve means that dealers will buy all Jumbo landings as long as the price of Jumbo is less than or equal to $p_J$. The same holds true for the Large market category. --->

These five assumptions have varying levels of realism.  Identical fish within a market category and a perfectly elastic demand curve are both unrealistic for many reasons.  However, we can control for many of these effects.  Black Sea Bass vary across many attributes, including size, method of production, landing date, and landing location.  Meat quality can vary within a season, resulting in different prices within a year.  Regional differences in transportation costs, processing costs, or final consumer preferences and incomes can produce regional variation in the demand curve for fish and therefore regional variation in *ex-vessel* prices [@samuelson1954transfer; @Krugman1991a].  The demand curve for nearly all fish is downward sloping: increases in quantity supplied will reduce prices [@Kristofersson2004; @Kristofersson2007; @Lee2014; @Ardini2018].  Our empirical classification model attempts to control for these effects by including explanatory factors that proxy for them.

In equation \@ref(unknown1), we developed the intuition behind the model using two market categories and note that we can deduce the composition of the unclassfied transactions based on the price.  Because there are four market categories for Black Sea Bass, equation \ref{unknown1} generalizes to:
\begin{equation}
\label{unknown2}
p_i^U= \alpha_{iJ} p^J + \alpha_{iL} p^L  + \alpha_{iM} p^M +  + (1-\alpha_{iJ}-\alpha_{iM}-\alpha_{iL}) p^S.
\end{equation}

Without additional information, the the $\alpha$ terms in the model are fundamentally underindentified. Any arbitrary price between $p_S$ and $p_J$ could be constructed with infinitely many weighted combinations of price. A strict application of this model will underestimate the level variability of the resultant length- or age- structure relative to the true, but unobserved, level.  For example, consider a transaction of Unclassified landings that trades at $p_L$ but is actually a mix of Medium and Jumbo.   Equation \ref{unknown2} classifies this a Large transaction and the length histograms of Medium, Large, and Jumbo fish in Figure \@ref(fig:LengthHistograms) illustrate the lower level of variability.

## Modeling Probability of Class Membership with a Random Forest

The Black Sea Bass stock assessment currently uses an age-structured estimate of the numbers of commercial landings aggregated at the year, semester, and subunit.  Therefore, our goal with the empirical model is to assign the Unclassified landings to one of the other four categories with good age and length data at the year-, semester-, and subunit- levels of aggregation. Neither the prediction accuracy of an individual transaction, individual kilogram of fish, nor the causal mechanisms by which one factor affects market category is of interest.  Machine learning approaches, like multinomial random forest used in this article, focus on accurate prediction of an outcome variable instead of the causal relationship between predictors and outcome [@Varian2014; @Mullainathan2017; @Athey2019].  These approaches have recently proliferated in fisheries, ecology, and economics [@Rubbens2023; @Kuhn2024; @Akselrud2024]. Applications include classifying fishing activity with Vessel Monitoring Systems or Automatic Identification Systems [@Russo2011], building predictive models of fishing vessel trip costs [@Chan2021] or prices [@francca2024price], and image processing [@Alvarez-Ellacuria2020 ; @Khan2023 ;  @Rankin2024 ;  @Vanaki2025].

We use a multinomial random forest model [@Breiman2001; @Malley2012] to model the probability that a transaction is in one of the four principal market categories^[Random forest applications of these models in fisheries include classification of acoustic data [@Fallon2016, @Proud2020], fishery metiers [@Oostdijk2024], and habitat [@Liu2025].].  Random Forests can be viewed as ensembles of Classification and Regression Trees [CART, @Breiman1984].  A classification tree repeatedly partitions observations into two groups based on a single explanatory variable.  The optimal variable and the value at which to partition is selected by minimizing a measure of variation among members of the resulting partitions; we use Gini impurity as this measure. The CART algorithm grows trees by continuing to split until all branches are homogeneous or an early stopping criterion is met. 

Single classification trees suffer from poor external validity because a tree grown to pure nodes is perfectly fit to the training dataset.  Random forests improve out of sample prediction by bootstrapping and restricting each bootstrap replication to a small number of randomly selected predictors [@Breiman2001; @Strobl2009; @Hastie2023].  Both modifications induce variation in the individual classification trees.  In the canonical version of the random forest, individual trees produce a prediction of class and the forest aggregates by a majority rule, the class with the most "votes" is the prediction  [@Breiman2001].  Motivated by Equation \ref{unknown2}, we treat the random forest as a probability machine by averaging over the final nodes of trees to assign probability of class membership [@Malley2012; @Kruppa2014].

Like many machine learning models, random forests have hyperparameters which must be exogenously supplied. Results can be sensitive to these choices; models are typically tuned by searching for an optimal set of parameters using a subset of data and the selected parameters are validated on a holdout sample.  Averaging methods, including Random Forest models, are also known to be underconfident; high probabilities are underestimated and low probabilities are overestimated.  This occurs because the model averaging process in which individual trees are aggregated into random forests averages away extreme values.  Calibration through an auxiliary model is often necessary after fitting a random forest [@Niculescu-Mizil2005; @Kull2017; @Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024; @Ferrer2025].

Our model training procedure attempts to account for the idiosyncrasies of Random Forest models and those of our data. Nearly all Random Forest applications tune the number of randomly selected predictors ($mtry$). Simulation studies by @Barreada2024 suggest tuning the minimum node size ($min_n$) when using random forests in probability models.  The observational units in our estimation dataset are the 545,000 transactions representing 20,217 metric tons (44.6 million pounds) of Black Sea Bass.  We treat the transactions as repeated observations of a pound of fish, and weight each observation by pounds landed as suggested by @solon2015.  The random forest model is fit in R using the ``ranger`` package; we use  ``tidymodels`` packages to facilitate tuning, training, and out-of-sample prediction^[https://www.tidymodels.org/. We purposefully chose to select from among mature, well-supported models that were part of this system because we hope to add this type of classification routine to ongoing stock assessments]. While random forest models in the ``tidymodels`` ecosystem support case weights, none fully supports our interpretation of frequency weighting.  Therefore, we overcome the problem with brute force by expanding our data to a large dataset with *pounds landed* copies of each row in which each row represents a single pound of fish.

During all stages when we split data and create folds, we ensure that all pounds from a transaction are placed into exactly one group.  However, during the bagging process of tree construction, observations can be partially in or out of an individual draw, therefore, we do not use the Out-of-Bag errors.  The *min_n* stopping parameter is now interpreted as the number of pounds in a node below which further splitting will not occur.  Because the expanded data is approximately 44 million rows and computing power is finite, we perform hyperparameter tuning on just a small subset of data.  We split our dataset into three parts: we use 80% of our dataset to train the model, 10% to calibrate probabilities, and 10% to validate the model.  We use 6.25% of the training sample (5% of the total dataset) to tune the model hyperparameters (just over 2.2 million rows from over 27,000 unique transactions).

We tune over these two hyperparameters by performing a 10-fold cross validation study in two steps. First, we grid search over the reasonable values of the two parameters.^[An initial grid search used a space filling grid and searched 24 points on $mtry \in [1,47]$ and $min_n \in [0,50000]$. The initial tuning results showed a relatively smooth surface and suggested the optimal $mtry<25$ and the optimal $min_n<2000$.  Second, a refined grid search was conducted over $mtry \in [8,32]$ and $min_n \in [10,2500]$].  We grow 200 trees during the tuning process.  Because tuning over a small part of our dataset risks identifying a suboptimal pair of hyperparameters, we draw a second, independent tuning set and tune again to verify the initial results. 

Our cross-validation folds are stratified by market category to ensure that the proportion of each class in the folds approximately matches the initial compositions.  We use the Brier Score, averaged over the ten folds, as the criterion function for tuning.

\begin{equation}
\label{brierscore}
BS = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=i}^N (Y_{ik}-Pr[Y_{ik}=1|X_i])^2
\end{equation}
where $i$ indexes observations, $k$ indexes classes, $Y_{ik}=1$ if observation $i$ is a member of class $k$, and $Pr_{ik}=1|X_i]$ is the predicted probability that observation $i$ is a member of class $k$ conditional on explanatory factors $X_i$.

After selecting a model, we train the final model on the 80% training dataset and grow 500 trees at this step. We use the trained model to predict class membership for the 10% calibration sample and visually assess whether the model is well-calibrated using commonly used calibration plots [@Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024].Unlike the commonly used isotonic and beta calibrations, the multinomial calibration does not require an ad-hoc adjustment to ensure that each observation's probabilities sum to one.  We also use the Relative Calibration loss methods described in @Ferrer2025 to characterize the gains from calibration.  We apply the trained model and the probability calibration routine to the final 10% of our data as a test of our model.  

## Out of Sample Predictions

We use the trained Random forest to predict the probability that Unclassified observations belong to each of the four classes.  We multiply these probabilities by the live weight of the transaction and aggregate these predicted live weights to the year-, market category-, subunit-, and semester level.  Similar to our treatment of the Random Forest as a probability machine, this approach is driven by Equation \ref{unknown2}.

The out of sample prediction itself is appropriate if there are no unobserved systematic differences between Unclassified and Classified fish that are not observed. There are a few ways that Unclassifieds this could occur.  One mechanism is if high-quality producers and dealers are more likely to grading into classes, perhaps because they earn higher returns from selling into a more sophisticated downstream market that is attuned to quality.  Alternatively, grading might only be performed in areas of the region or times of the year when the premium for larger fish is high.  Both of these effect would be difficult to control for. We control the for dealer quality effects, price premia, and region or time, by including relevant explanatory factors. However, a change in the relationship between these factors and the market category cannot be modeled.

## Constructing an Age Structure

We applied the length- and age- expansion process used in the 2024 Black Sea Bass stock assessment to calculate the landings-at-age. We construct a "price informed" landings at age structure by substituting in the random forest predictions for the Unclassified fish. 

# Data, Pre-Processing, and Feature Engineering

We use Catch Accounting and Monitoring System (CAMS)^[Documentation at https://apps-garfo.fisheries.noaa.gov/cams/index.html] data from 2013 to 2025 to train our model, this represents 20,483.5 metric tons of Classified fish of worth just over \$150M real USD. The CAMS data consists of dealer transactions matched to vessel trip reports. Dealer data are transaction-level reports of fish purchases by federally permitted fish dealers from each vessel. Dealers may buy from many vessels on a day and vessels may sell to multiple dealers on a day.  These reports are disaggregated to the trip and market category level and include landed weight (pounds) and value (nominal US Dollars).  Prices are converted to real (First quarter of 2023) values using the CPI for all urban consumers (CPIAUCSL). Vessel trip report data are reports of fishing activity by federally permitted vessels that are disaggregated to the statistical area-gear-trip level and include information about area fished, gear used, trip length, and estimates of both quantity kept and discarded at the species level.   Matching is performed based on the Vessel trip report serial number. When this match fails,  CAMS uses the vessel permit number, dealer identifier, and date  to link vessel reports and the dealer reports.  When vessels fish in multiple statistical areas, they file more than one report per trip.  For these types of trips, the CAMS data system allocates trip-level landings to the appropriate statistical area in proportion to the hail weights on those trip reports, splitting a single trip record into multiple observations.  The Black Sea Bass stock assessment is spatially explicit, and the statistical area is used to assign all landings to either the North or South subunit.

Black Sea Bass may be caught by firms without a federal fishing permit and sold to dealers without a federal dealer permit.  In some states, firms without a federal permit can fish for Black Sea Bass in state waters (within 3 miles of land) and sell it to fish dealers who do not have a federal permit.  These sales are also in our data and CAMS imputes both statistical area (area adjacent to landing port) and gear used when missing. 
Economic theory described in the theoretical model and on-the-ground subject-matter expertise (the Black Sea Bass stock assessment and commercial fishery) guide explanatory factors, factor engineering, selection of data, and validation procedures [@Mullainathan2017]. The dependent variable is the market category. Machine learning algorithms can often benefit from preprocessing data and factor engineering. Missing values for predictors are handled by splitting the data as if they did not exist, assigning the observations with missing values to each nodes, and selecting the node that has the greatest decrease in impurity.  We treat factor variables as "unordered" and follow the implementation method described in @Hastie2009.  Unlike many other machine learning models, Random Forest models are scale invariant; explanatory factors do not need to be centered at zero or scaled to have similar variances. 

We operationalize the Law of One Price by constructing a "prevailing price" for each market category at the state level by constructing a weighted moving average over the previous 14 days.  Implicit in the construction of a state-level prevailing price, is the assumption that each state represents a distinct market. While overly restrictive (fish landing in Delaware and Maryland probably are part of the same market), this allows the classifier to account for the fact that the prevailing prices do differ across states (See Appendix Figure \@ref(fig:HedonicMarginals)).

There are some periods where no sales are observed for a particular market category, state, and day. When this occurs, we impute a prevailing price based on the regional price for the market category and each state's average premium or discount to that regional price.  We enter the difference between a transaction's price and the prevailing price for Jumbo, Large, and Medium market classes. We do not include a price difference relative to Small for two reasons. First, landings of Small are relatively infrequent, so constructing a prevailing small price could introduce more noise and degrade model fit. Second, small fish are likely to have the lowest prices and the difference with respect to Medium will capture this phenomenon without using an additional factor. During the model specification search, we also experimented with including raw prices. 

The buyers (dealers) are the entities that report the market category of fish and are likely to have an unobserved propensity to grade fish into particular classes.  Traditional estimators often use a set of one-hot indicator variables to account for individual-specific effects; applying this method to Random Forests can lead to both overfitting [@Breiman2001; @Hastie2023] and bias [@Strobl2007; @Strobl2009]. Target-encoding collapses these indicators to one per class and minimizes this problem. In this application, we adjust the typical target-encoding procedure by constructing annual, dealer-specific weighted class shares and enter these, lagged one year, as predictors. We also add a "first year" variable for the first year that a dealer is seen purchasing Black Sea Bass in our database and code the dealer-specific effects as missing. 

Table \@ref(tab:tbl-cont-weightedA) summarizes our continuous economic variables, including prices, transaction sizes, trip-level landings, price differences, and dealer propensities.  We note that Jumbo and Large fish tend to be landed in greater quantities than Medium or Small and on trips that land more fish.  Patterns in the price difference variables are expected: the price of Jumbos tends to be close to the prevailing price of Jumbos. In contrast the price of Smalls is lower than every other category.  Our dealer propensity measures illustrate that Jumbo and Large transactions tend to be purchased by dealers who specialize in those two categories, while buyers of Medium and Small tend to be more generalist Black Sea Bass purchasers.

In addition to prices and variables that explain prices, we include variables that proxy for production processes and biological availability. Together, this includes controls for gear, subunit, grade, management system, state only permit, and semester (Table \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-timeA) and \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-methodA) ). Table \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-methodA) summarizes the controls for method of production, and the proportion of landings in each category varies greatly by gear and subunit, and minimally by grade, management system, shore, state-only permits, and semester.  The monthly patterns illustrate some seasonality, with Jumbos being more prevalent in winter and spring (December through April) and both Small and Medium being more prevalent in summer (May -July). These likely reflect a combination of biological availability, regulatory availability, and targeting capability that varies across the fishing fleet. Finally, the state percentages are striking for Small, with 58\% of RI and 30\% of VA landings being in the small market category. 

We also construct additional proxies for biological availability from the 7 day moving average of landings at the subunit, state, and gear for each of the four market categories. The intuition here is that the stock of fish in the ocean is a public good that firms use as an input to produce landings. Catch is likely to be correlated across firms that use the same resource and these moving averages of catch control for the public good. We also include proxies for the current day's landings and trips by other firms^[We *exclude* landings or effort associated with the transaction]. To provide a concrete example, if vessel *a* lands Black Sea Bass during a time period when many trips by other vessels are landing a large quantity of Jumbo Black Sea Bass, then vessel $a$'s transaction is more likely to be Jumbo as well. Descriptive statistics for these proxies are presented in Appendix  \@ref(AppendixDataSummaries). 

The theoretical model sketch guides both the types of explanatory factors used in the model and the observations of data used to train the Random Forest. Observations with prices are formed in a manner inconsistent with our theoretical model are removed  from the training dataset.  Of the 20,484.5mt of Black Sea Bass in our estimation sample, we exclude 267mt (1.3\%) for three reasons. 

First, there is less quality assurance and quality control for the species value field which we use to construct prices. While there are checks to ensure that the values are within a reasonable range, firms that do not report accurately may not be required to improve their reporting accuracy. We handle this by excluding transactions with prices that are too high (over \$15 per pound) or too low (under \$0.15 per pound).  Second, buyers and sellers may be owned by the same entity; when this happens, the reported *ex-vessel* prices are likely to be insensitive to market forces and not reflect a market equilibrium price.  Fully disentangling ownership is difficult, but inspection of the data suggested that some dealer-vessel pairs were exclusively trading with each other, suggesting some vertical integration.  Third, firms may also participate in forward contracting in which the price of fish is determined well in advance of landing.  To account  for the final two, we excluded transactions from dealer-year-market category combinations where the standard deviation of prices was less than 0.10.  We did not notice a pattern in the excluded data across market categories; Small were slightly less likely to be excluded by these three criteria.   

The fact that buyers may have an unobserved propensity to either buy or grade fish into particular classes and the potential effect this has on cross-validation is worth discussing.  @Roberts2017 note that standard cross-validation techniques are overly optimistic when observations are dependent.  This occurs because the hold out data used for cross-validation is not actually independent. @Roberts2017 suggest that the practical implications of this depend on the purposes of the model; if prediction on "similar" data is the goal, then a standard cross-validation may be appropriate.  We believe this is the case in our analysis: we observe records of sales from vessels to dealers, train our model on a subset (the non-Unclassified transactions) of those data, and predict out of sample on the remaining Unclassified transactions. At every point in the process, including when we predict out of sample, we are able to observe the dealer and its propensity to grade or purchase each of the market categories^[If, however, our objective was to predict class membership for new dealers, the standard cross validation could lead to overly optimistic training results and poor out of sample prediction].  

In order for the out-of-sample predictions to be valid, the underlying data generating process for both Unclassifieds and  Classified fish must be the same.  Equivalently, conditional on all explanatory factors in our classification model, there is no difference between a 

This could happen if classification is only done by producers with high-quality products that also take better care of their fish after the catch. It could also happen if the extra handling needed to classify fish causes some damage and reduces quality.  We attempt to control for those possible differences by including explanatory factors that may be correlated with quality, and therefore prices, in the model.  There are two covariate shifts that are worth noting: Unclassifieds are more likely to be landed in New York and Delaware (Table  \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-timeA)) and landed by state-only permitted firms  (Table  \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-methodA)).

To summarize our modeling approach, we expand our transaction data up to pounds and tune two hyperaparameters using a small portion (5\%) of our dataset with a 10-fold cross-validation. The model includes controls for prices, economic activity, and biological availability. After hyperparameter tuning, we train the model on 80\% of the data, fit a multinomial calibration using a 10\% sample, and test the model on the final 10\% holdout sample.   We use the trained model to predict out-of-sample on the unclassified (1,632 mt) Black Sea Bass and aggregate to the subunit-year-semester.  In our data cleaning step, we exclude certain observations from our estimation sample, notably observations from dealers that exhibit little variation in prices, when we apply the same filters, we are left with 1,064mt of Black Sea bass.


# Results

The set of tuning parameters with the lowest Brier score were $mtry=14$ and $min_n=10$ ($BS=0.1783$).  However, we opted to use the second best set of hyperparameters  ($mtry=15, min_n=896;BS=0.1792$) for two reasons.  The first is computational; models with larger $min_n$ fit more rapidly and use less memory, because fewer splits are performed. Second, a model with very low $min_n$ may perform poorly out of sample due to overfitting. While $min_n=10$ is not particularly low for standard random forest, the rows in our expanded dataset represent a single pound of landings.  A very small $min_n$ may produce many terminal nodes containing observations from a single transaction which would lead to overfitting.  Inspection of the tuning surface revealed that the model fit was not particularly sensitive to a large portion of the hyperparameter space that we evaluated (See Appendix \@ref(AppendixRFFit)). 

The calibration steps find moderate gain from multinomial calibration, and the validation shows the model fits well. The tuning and validation model fit statistics are similar, suggesting the model is not overfit.  Although the model is not a causal one, the importance of explanatory factors in the Variable Importance Plots makes intuitive sense; prices and dealer-specific effects are important factors in the classification model.

## Tuning, Calibration, and Test Results

The ROC curves from tuning characterize the tradeoff between correctly predicting a class (true positive) and incorrectly predicting that class (false positive) by adjusting the threshold for class prediction.  They are similar across folds and the initial steepness indicates even with a very small subset of data, the tuned Random Forest model can distinguish between the four principal market categories (Figure  \@ref(fig:rocTune)).  Despite the Small market category being relatively rare in the data, the random forest does quite well at distinguishing Small from other categories. The model performs worst at classifying the Large market category; Figure \@ref(fig:LengthHistograms) illustrates the relatively high degree of overlap between the prices of Large with its neighboring Medium and Jumbo market categories.  

We apply the final trained model to the test set to construct the ROC curve in Figure  \@ref(fig:roc-Valid). The general shape of Figure \@ref(fig:roc-Valid) is similar to that of the individual folds from tuning, suggesting we are not overfitting the model^[Tuning is performed on 5\% of the dataset, but final model training uses 80\% of the data. Therefore, simply by using much more data, we expect model fit to improve.].  

The left panel of Figure \@ref(fig:calibrationplots) illustrates an issue that commonly affects predictions of Random Forest models. These plots are constructed by plotting moving windows of predicted probabilities of the test set on the x-axis against the observed outcomes on the y-axis.  Well-calibrated models have plots that are close to the 45-degree line.  For all four classes, the aggregation of individual trees leads to the  sigmoidal underconfidence curve in which observations with high predicted probabilities have even higher true probabilities.

To correct this, we fit an auxiliary multinomial probability calibration to the holdout sample.   The calibration improves predicted probabilities visually (Right panel of Figure \@ref(fig:calibrationplots)) and the Brier Score on the test set slightly. 

The Variable Importance Plot confirms that the three price difference variables are quite impactful in predicting market category (Figure \@ref(fig:vip)), as are the transaction weight, trip level landings, proxies for availability at various levels, and the dealer propensities to purchase various sizes. Again, we caution against interpreting the ability to predict as a causal mechanism.

We also construct a weighted confusion matrix based on the calibrated model predictions (Figure \@ref(fig:SoftWeightedPredictionHeatmap)).  For each observation in the test set, we multiply landed weight by each of the class membership probabilities and then aggregate.  The model correctly classifies 82\% of Jumbo, 78\% of Large, 81\% of Medium, and 76\% of Small landings. Reassuringly, the model incorrect predictions, located in the off-diagonal terms of Figure \@ref(fig:SoftWeightedPredictionHeatmap), nearly offset each other.  Consider the true Jumbo market category. The off-diagonal terms in the top row show that our Random Forest incorrectly classifies 103 mt of Jumbo as Large, 20 mt as Medium, and 1mt as Small.  This aggregate prediction error is mostly offset by the 80 mt of true Large and 10 mt of true Medium that are incorrectly classified as Jumbo.  Table \@ref(tab:weighted-predictions) illustrates that the Calibrated Random Forest predictions are quite accurate at predicting weights by market category.  Somewhat surprisingly, Table \@ref(tab:transaction-predictions) illustrates that the trained model is better at predicting aggregate transactions than weights.

##  Out of Sample Predictions

In our data cleaning step, we exclude certain observations from our estimation sample; Figure \@ref(fig:out-of-sample-preds) illustrates graphically these predictions when we refrain from predicting market category for similar observations. Figure \@ref(fig:ambitious-out-of-sample-preds) requires all unclassified transactions to be predicted into another market category. The hedonic model suggested the Unclassified fish are likely to be a mix of Medium and Large fish (Table \ref{HedonicMarketCats}) and the histograms of both prices and lengths suggested more heterogeneity.  Figures \@ref(fig:out-of-sample-preds) and \@ref(fig:ambitious-out-of-sample-preds) generally agree with those exploratory analyses: the Unclassified fish are mostly predicted to be in the Medium or Large market category but there are some predictions of Jumbos and Smalls, particularly in the North subunit.

##  Catch-at-age Frequencies


The price-informed classification produced minimal differences in our understanding of landings-at-age of the Unclassified Black Sea Bass in the North subunit (Figure \@ref(fig:CAA-comparison-UNC-only)).  There are year-to-year differences between the methods, but no obvious patterns.  We interpret agreement between the Original and Price-Informed distribution of landings as corroborating evidence that the model fits well.  Length and age information for the Unclassified category was collected from the North subunit through 2020, however the total number of samples is relatively small (Figure \@ref(LenHist2)). By reallocating landings out of the Unclassified category, the price-informed age structure does not use that sparse data at all. Both the price-informed and original age structure of show cohort effects: age-2 fish make up a large proportion of North catch in 2014, with the peaks moving down and right over time. A similar cohort effect begins in 2018 and a smaller one in 2021.

In the South subunit, the price-informed classifier produces a greater proportion of younger (age 2-4) landings-at-age and a smaller proportion of older (ages 5-7) than in the original data.  This is the empirical result that is relevant for the stock assessment process.  Interestingly, the cohort effects are far less pronounced in the price-informed South age structure.  




# Discussion

This effort illustrates a novel method of using socioeconomic information in the data processing step of the stock assessment enterprise.  Economic information (prices) collected at the level of a sales transaction is  used as a substitute for biological samples that were not collected.  This method could be adapted to other settings where prices are the result of a competitive market and are routinely collected.  In the Northeast United States, this method was applied using readily-available, historical data; it did not require collection of additional data or manually processing historically collected data. We note some caveats to the method and areas for followup research.

### More that two market categories

When there are more than two market categories (say, Medium), equation \ref{unknown1} becomes:

\begin{align}
p&= \beta_1 p^J+ \beta_2 p^L + (1-\beta_1-\beta_2) \\\label{unknown2}
\sum_{i=1}^3 \beta_i&=1\\
\geq 0 & \beta_i \geq 1 \hspace{2mm} \forall i=1,2
\end{align}
Intuitively, observing a transaction price that falls between two market categories does not imply that a transaction is a linear combination of the two adjacent categories. This suggests that including other proxies for beyond just prices and factors that affect prices is necessary.

Using a model to predict out of sample always comes with concerns about external validity.  A parallel to the random sampling process used to collect age- and length data using portside samplers is used as comparision.  Filling missing length- or age- data from another neighboring strata is a simple out-of-sample prediction: that the donor strata is identical to the missing strata.  The most recent Black Sea Bass stock assessment used contemporaneous North subunit data as a donor for missing South subunit data for eight years.  It used a single year, 2020, of North subunit data as a donor for both subunits from 2020 to 2024.  Many Northeast US groundfish stocks use "all classified combined" as a donor for missing Unclassifieds.  

These "unconditional" predictions do not make adjustments for any differences in observables.  As an example, Unclassified Black Sea Bass are more likely to be landed in New York and Delaware (Table \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-timeA))  by state-only permitted firms fishing in nearshore areas  (Table  \@ref(tab:print-tbl-cat-methodA)).  Spatial variation in life history and biological availability may cause the representativeness assumption to break down: nearshore Black Sea Bass are could to be different from deeper water Black Sea Bass.

The classification model attempts to condition on those factors and prices emerge as the strongest differentiators of market category.  We train the model on Classified observations and then predict out of sample on Unclassified.   A related, but slightly different assumption, is required for the out of sample prediction to be valid. The fact that Unclassifieds are more likely to be landed in New York and Delaware by state-only permitted firms is not a problem for external validity as long as the relationship between these explanatory factors and the market category is consistent for both the classified categories and the Unclassified fish.

This is reasonable if, as we assume, Unclassifieds are simply a mix of different classes and an efficient market for fish exists. In particular, it assumes that the Unclassifieds can, and are, costlessly classified by the dealer and sold downstream.  This may not be strictly true; it costs time to sort fish, although the marginal cost of sorting borne by the dealer may be minimal.  However, there are also mechanisms by which the Unclassifieds may be systematically different from the Classified fish.  For example, classification might only be done by producers with high-quality products that also take better care of their fish after the catch. 

Footnote \ref{aggregation_footnote_label} notes that some minor market categories (Extra Small, Pee-Wee, and Extra Large) were aggregated into more prevalent ones, maintaining the "unconditional representativeness" assumption. This could be revisited relatively easily by excluding types of observations from the estimation dataset, retraining the Random Forest, and predicting out of sample on these observations. We chose not to do this to focus on the data gap caused by lack of sampling.

Another caveat is that the Random Forest implementation does not account for the ordinal relationship between the size classes. Although there is overlap in the length distributions (a particular Jumbo fish might be smaller than a Large), the size categories themselves are ordered, and models that account for this ordering may perform better [@lechner2025].

In addition to the above caveats, one other about generalization is warranted. Black Sea Bass prices are approximately monotone in size; larger fish have higher prices.  Using prices as an additional source of information would be difficult if there were a non-monotone relationship between size and prices.  If, after conditioning for other factors that influence prices, buyers were willing to pay similar prices for both Jumbo and Small fish, then using prices to predict market category would likely assign high priced transactions to these two categories. This could produce poor downstream predictions of Numbers-at-Length or Numbers-at-age needed for stock assessment.

Our Random Forest model does well at predicting observations and comparatively worse at weights (Tables \@ref(tab:weighted-predictions) and \@ref(tab:transaction-predictions)).  This is a bit surprising:  we expand our data to treat a landed pound of fish as the observational unit and expected the opposite to occur.  Because our primary interest here is predictions of aggregate weights, the quantification methods described by @milli2013quantification and @gonzalez2017review may improve predictive power.

The difference between the original and price-informed landings-at-age structures in the South subunit (Figure \@ref(fig:CAA-comparison-UNC-only)) is not unexpected.  The exploratory analysis in Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) illustrates that fish in a market category tend to be slightly larger in the North relative to the South.  Therefore, simply applying the North age structure of Unclassified landings to the South would likely overestimate the proportion of older fish in the South landings. By using the information contained in prices to reclassify the Unclassified market category into Jumbo, Large, Medium, or Small, we can improve upon approached used to fill data gaps in the most recent stock assessment.  

Because the proportion of total landings in the Unclassified category is relatively small (around 10% of commercial landings), the change in the age structure of commercial landings supplied to the stock assessment is also minimal.   Black Sea Bass removals also include commercial discards, recreational landings, and discards (See Figure \@ref(fig:CAA-comparison-all) in the Appendix).  However, the perspective of the size and age of individuals in the unclassified market category is markedly different between the two methods.  It is vital to be able to track shifts in Black Sea Bass biology to perceive changes in condition (i.e., if the average length or weight is fluctuating), and using a classification method that uses all available information helps understand this picture. 

# Conclusions
This effort uses socioeconomic information in a novel way in the stock assessment process to improve our understanding of commercial removals. More ambitiously, our work also suggests a method for optimizing the portside collection of  biological data. Collecting samples is costly. The information contained in prices could substitute for some of this costly data and allow this sampling effort to be reallocated to other market categories, stocks, or species. Candidates for reduced sampling include difficult-to-sample categories when there is size overlap with neighboring categories.  Again, we note that a successful empirical setting would include prices that depend approximately monotonically on size and competitive markets for fish. We specifically caution against forgoing age-sampling on "terminal" size market categories (Jumbo and Small in the case of Black Sea Bass).  

A prospective change to a sampling structure could be investigated by training a classifier without a particular market category. For Black Sea Bass, we exclude the Unclassified and then predict out of sample. To investigate the effects of forgoing sampling of the Large class, we could train a classifier on the Small, Medium, and Jumbo classes, predict the class membership of the Large classes, combine the resultant predicted weights with the known lengths and ages of the other three classes and compare to the known age and length structure of the Large class.  We leave this to future research.


\clearpage

```{r validation-predictions-prep, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

aggregate_transactions<-nocluster_testing_predictions %>%
    summarise(across(c(starts_with(".pred_")), sum)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols=starts_with(".pred_"), names_to="market_desc", names_prefix=".pred_",values_to="predicted_transactions")


aggregate_test_predictions<-nocluster_testing_predictions %>%
    summarise(across(c(starts_with("pred_")), sum)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols=starts_with("pred_"), names_to="market_desc", names_prefix="pred_",values_to="predicted")


true<-nocluster_testing_predictions %>%
    group_by(market_desc) %>%
    summarise(lndlb=sum(lndlb),
              transactions=sum(transactions))

Testmkt_preds<-aggregate_transactions %>%
  left_join(true, by=join_by(market_desc==market_desc))

Testmkt_preds<-Testmkt_preds %>%
  left_join(aggregate_test_predictions, by=join_by(market_desc==market_desc))

Testmkt_preds<-Testmkt_preds %>%
  mutate(predicted=predicted/lbs_per_mt,
         lndlb=lndlb/lbs_per_mt) %>%
  rename(true_mt=lndlb,
         predicted_mt=predicted)%>%
  mutate(`mt error (%)`=percent((predicted_mt-true_mt)/true_mt, accuracy=0.01),
         `Transaction error (%)` = percent((predicted_transactions-transactions)/transactions, accuracy=0.01) )

# Just keep a few columns and polish them up to look nice in the manuscript.
transaction_predictions<-Testmkt_preds %>%
  select(market_desc,transactions, predicted_transactions, `Transaction error (%)`) %>%
    mutate(
    predicted_transactions = comma(predicted_transactions, accuracy = 1),
    transactions = comma(transactions, accuracy = 1)                        
  )
```


\clearpage
